nameStory: The 'monkeyflower' name comes from the flower's amusing resemblance to a monkey's face - the two-lipped petals create what looks like a grinning simian expression. The 'sharpwing' part refers to the distinctive winged ridges that run down the plant's square stems, giving them sharp edges you can feel with your fingers.
description: Sharpwing monkeyflower is a cheerful wetland perennial that brightens soggy spots with blue to violet monkey-faced flowers from summer into early fall. This fast-growing plant reaches about 2-4 feet tall and spreads readily in wet conditions. Its square, winged stems and opposite leaves make it easy to spot even when not blooming, and it has a relatively short lifespan compared to most perennials.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems with distinctive sharp, wing-like ridges running down each corner that you can easily feel with your thumb - these wings are what give the plant its 'sharpwing' name

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Blue to violet two-lipped flowers that really do look like tiny monkey faces grinning at you - the upper lip has two lobes, the lower lip has three, and they have no noticeable scent

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves (paired across from each other on the stem) that are green and relatively smooth to the touch, attached directly to the stem without stalks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies in wet areas through spreading roots, creating patches of upright stems that sway gently in the breeze near water sources

habitat: Look for sharpwing monkeyflower in wet meadows, along stream banks, pond edges, and other consistently moist to wet soils throughout New England. It thrives in areas that stay soggy or even occasionally flood, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other water-loving plants in full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from spreading roots, with the distinctive winged square stems becoming visible as they grow rapidly in wet spring conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with blue-violet monkey-faced flowers opening from June onward, creating colorful displays in wetland areas.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering into September, with seed capsules developing and eventually releasing tiny seeds before the plant dies back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground parts visible until the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called a 'monkeyflower,' this plant produces flowers with absolutely no scent at all - unusual for such colorful blooms that seem designed to attract attention!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close cousin Allegheny monkeyflower, but sharpwing has much more pronounced wing-ridges on its stems that feel sharp to the touch, while Allegheny monkeyflower's stems have only slight ridges. Memory trick: 'Sharp'-wing has the 'sharp' ridges you can really feel.
contextualKnowledge: With only 32 recorded observations in New England, this is one of our less common monkeyflowers - you're more likely to encounter the similar but more widespread Allegheny monkeyflower in most wetland areas.
compareHints: Compared to Allegheny monkeyflower, sharpwing monkeyflower has much more pronounced winged ridges on its stems that feel distinctly sharp when you run your finger along them. Both have similar blue-violet monkey-faced flowers and grow in wet areas, but the stem wings are the key difference - Allegheny monkeyflower's stems have only subtle ridges that are barely noticeable to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Allegheny monkeyflower can be distinguished from its close relative, sharpwing monkeyflower, by its stalkless leaves that clasp the stem directly.
